hops.title: Bacteria that carry electrons through centimeters of mud
hops.text: In mitochondrial Complex I, a run of several electron hops spans about ten nanometers in all. On the muddy seafloor, cable bacteria carry electrons across a centimeter or more, roughly a million times farther. Identified in Denmark in 2012, each is a long chain of cells reaching up through the mud. Deep down there is sulfide but no oxygen; at the top there is oxygen. Cells at the bottom strip electrons from sulfide and send them up conductive protein fibers in the shared cell envelope to cells near the surface, which hand them to oxygen. Those fibers conduct about as well as highly doped synthetic conducting polymers.

sources.citation: Pfeffer C, Larsen S, Song J, et al. Filamentous bacteria transport electrons over centimetre distances. Nature. 2012;491:218-221.
van der Veen JR, Hidalgo Martinez S, Wieland A, et al. ACS Nano. 2024;18(47):32878-32889.

Sazanov LA, Hinchliffe P. Structure of the hydrophilic domain of respiratory complex I from Thermus thermophilus. Science. 2006;311:1430-1436 (iron-sulfur chain about 95 angstroms long); reviewed in Sazanov LA. Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol. 2015;16:375-388.

hops.title: The oxygen you breathe in is made into water
hops.text: Ask a roommate where inhaled oxygen goes, and many will say it leaves as carbon dioxide. Not directly. That CO₂ comes from breaking down food. Most of the O₂ your cells use goes to Complex IV, picks up electrons and protons, and becomes water. In 1949, two mice and a rat given heavy oxygen to breathe showed it in their body water, and some reached their exhaled CO₂ by swapping atoms with that water. At rest you make about 250 to 350 milliliters of metabolic water a day, mostly this way. Kangaroo rats, which almost never drink, make about half a gram of water per gram of dry seeds burned.

hops.afterHeading: Two machines that keep each other in step
hops.title: How a World War I munitions chemical became a 1930s diet drug
hops.text: During World War I, French factories used 2,4-dinitrophenol, DNP, to make munitions. In 1933, Maurice Tainter at Stanford reported that the same chemical raised people's metabolic rate and caused rapid weight loss, and it was soon sold over the counter without a prescription. The reason is this section's uncoupler. DNP lets protons leak back across the inner membrane, so the chain races, fuel burns faster, less of its energy is captured as ATP, and more leaves as heat. People developed cataracts, and some died of overheating. Doctors stopped prescribing it once the harm was clear, and a 1938 federal law finally let regulators act against its sellers.

sources.citation: Grundlingh J, Dargan PI, El-Zanfaly M, Wood DM. 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP): a weight loss agent with significant acute toxicity and risk of death. J Med Toxicol. 2011;7(3):205-212.
